A resolution passed at the All-India Muslim League's meeting in Lahore on 23 March 1940, calling for "independent states" in the areas of India where Muslims were in the majority. It is seen as the start of the demand for Pakistan, though the word was not in it.

It was proposed by Bengal's A. K. Fazlul Huq and backed by others. In his speech, Muhammad Ali Jinnah argued that Hindus and Muslims were two nations, not two communities, with different religions, laws and ways of life. This two-nation idea marked a shift from his earlier years as a champion of Hindu-Muslim unity, a shift that grew after the Congress ministries of 1937 to 1939, when he felt Muslims were shut out of power.

Opponents ridiculed it, and Hindu newspapers called it the "Pakistan Resolution". Within seven years it was the League's main aim. The text said "states", in the plural, and was vague on borders, which later mattered a great deal.

It led, by way of the 1946 riots, to the Partition in 1947.
